objection: If Jesus is God, why did he pray to God?
answer:
Thank you for asking this so honestly — it's exactly the right question to sit with, not brush past, because the Gospels really do show Jesus praying, thanking the Father, asking for help. The key is that "Jesus is God" was never meant to mean "Jesus is the Father" or "Jesus is a solitary divine person talking to himself." From the beginning, orthodox Christian faith confesses one God in three distinct, co-equal, co-eternal persons — Father, Son, and Spirit. The Son is truly God, of one nature with the Father, but he is a distinct person from the Father. So when Jesus prays in the garden or gives thanks before the five thousand, the eternal Son is speaking to the Father — a real, personal address between two who are truly distinct in person while being one in being. This is not play-acting. John 17, for instance, shows Jesus asking the Father to glorify him with the glory he had with the Father before the world existed — which itself presupposes his eternal divine standing, even as it distinguishes him personally from the Father he addresses (John 17:3-5).

And here's the crucial point about the human nature: the Son didn't just wear a costume of humanity — he actually took to himself a real, full human nature, with a genuine human mind, will, and dependence, without ceasing to be God. So the prayers are not evidence against his deity; they're the natural voice of true humanity united to true divinity in one person. That's precisely what the phrase "the Father is greater" and "not my will, but thine" are getting at: the incarnate Son, as man, submits to and depends on the Father, even while remaining, as God, one in nature with him. Notice that the very Gospel most full of this dependent prayer language — John — is the one that opens by calling the Word God (John 1:1) and closes with Thomas kneeling before the risen Christ confessing, "My Lord and my God" (John 20:28). So the writer clearly did not think the prayers undercut the deity; he placed both side by side without embarrassment, because in his mind they were never in tension. Far from fooling anyone, this is why the earliest Jewish Christians — people who would rather die than worship a creature — began calling on Jesus in prayer themselves, as in Stephen's dying words, "Lord Jesus, receive my spirit" (Acts 7:59), and the ancient prayer Maranatha, "our Lord, come" (1 Corinthians 16:22). They had watched him pray to the Father and still concluded he was worthy of the very worship reserved for God alone.

If Jesus *is* God—truly God, not just a really godly person—then who exactly was he praying to in the garden, or when he thanked his Father before feeding the five thousand? It seems like he was talking to someone *other than* himself, asking them for help. And I know people say "he was human too," but doesn't that just sound like he was playing a role? I'm not trying to be difficult—I just need to know: is there a way to read all of this that doesn't make it sound like Jesus was either not really God, or was fooling everyone about who he was talking to?
